headline_en: New opportunity for sending workers to Malaysia
summary_en: On 28 October 2025 Malaysia sent Bangladesh a 10-point 'Recruiting Agent Selection Criteria' for private agencies that may send workers to Malaysia, following the third Joint Working Group meeting in Dhaka on 21-22 May. The ministry says the same criteria will apply to Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan and Myanmar, and asked licensed agencies that meet them to apply to the ministry by 7 November 2025.

facts.statement: On Tuesday 28 October 2025 the Malaysian government sent Bangladesh its 'Recruiting Agent Selection Criteria' for choosing private recruiting agents to send workers to Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: At the third Bangladesh-Malaysia Joint Working Group meeting held in Dhaka on 21 and 22 May (2025), the Malaysian side promised to set criteria for selecting private recruiting agents, after Bangladesh asked Malaysia to include all valid licensed agents to keep parity with other sending countries.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Previously fewer Bangladeshi recruiting agencies got the chance to send workers to Malaysia compared with other sending countries; the ministry says the same selection criteria will in future apply to Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan and Myanmar.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 1 for Bangladeshi recruiting agencies: at least five years of satisfactory operation after getting the licence.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 2: proof of having sent at least 3,000 workers abroad in the last five years.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 3: experience of sending and placing workers in at least three different destination countries within the last five years.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 4: the agency must hold valid licences from all relevant Bangladeshi authorities for training, assessment, recruitment and overseas employment.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 5: the agency must have a good-conduct certificate from the proper authority of the sending country.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 6: the agency must have no record of involvement in forced labour recruitment, human trafficking, labour law violations, extortion of money, money laundering or other financial crime, or unethical migration practices.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 7: the agency must have its own training and assessment centre with full facilities, including accommodation, technical training facilities and an orientation module.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 8: the agency must have testimonials from five separate international employers saying it carried out migration activities satisfactorily.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 9: the agency must have a permanent office of at least 10,000 square feet, operated for at least three years, with infrastructure for selecting and recruiting workers.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Malaysia criterion 10: the agency must have proof that it previously followed the destination country's (including Malaysia's) recruitment conditions lawfully and procedurally when sending workers abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Bangladeshi licensed recruiting agents able to meet Malaysia's selection criteria were asked to apply with the supporting documents to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment by 7 November 2025; the Bangladesh government will then ask Malaysia to list every agent that meets the conditions without exception.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

headline_en: Scholarships for meritorious children of expatriate workers, applications close 25 November
summary_en: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board (under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment) will give education scholarships to children of expatriate workers. The article lists the GPA thresholds for SSC 2025, HSC 2024 and Diploma in Engineering 2024, the documents required, the scholarship duration, and the online application deadline of 25 November 2025.

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board will give education scholarships to children of expatriate workers; it is a scholarship of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship, SSC and equivalent 2025: children of workers currently working abroad need GPA 5.00 in science or GPA 4.75 in humanities and business studies; children of workers who died abroad need GPA 4.00 in science, humanities or business studies.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship, HSC and equivalent 2024: children of workers currently abroad need GPA 4.80 in science or GPA 4.50 in humanities and business studies; children of workers who died abroad need GPA 4.00 in any of the three groups.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship, Diploma in Engineering 2024: children of workers currently abroad need GPA 3.50; children of workers who died abroad need GPA 3.00.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Documents required for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship: proof that the mother or father is an expatriate worker; a certificate from the head of the educational institution including his or her mobile number; for children of workers who died abroad, a certificate from the embassy; a statement of the student's account at any bank with account number and routing number; one copy of the student's photo and signature; a copy of the student's NID card.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Duration of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship: SSC-category awardees get it for two years through classes 11 and 12, or four years if studying a diploma; HSC-category awardees get three years for a pass degree, four years for an honours degree and five years for medical; Diploma in Engineering awardees get four years.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

facts.statement: Applications for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship must be made online; the online application deadline is 25 November 2025. (The article's application link and website address are not printed in the text.)
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship notice

headline_en: Allegation of taking 5 times the fixed fee to send workers to Malaysia; cases against 13 companies
summary_en: On Sunday 14 September 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC/Dudok) filed cases against 31 people (chairmen, managing directors and directors) of 13 overseas recruiting companies for allegedly embezzling BDT 1,159 crore by charging Malaysia-bound workers five times the government-fixed BDT 78,990 through a syndicate. With earlier cases against 12 companies, the ACC has now acted in 25 cases against 64 accused over about BDT 2,288 crore.

facts.statement: The government-fixed cost for a Bangladeshi worker going to Malaysia was BDT 78,990, according to the ACC.
The ACC alleges that a syndicate of recruiting agency owners took five times the government-fixed BDT 78,990 from Malaysia-bound workers, taking extra money at various stages outside the agreement.

On Sunday 14 September 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission (Dudok) filed cases against 31 people, including chairmen, managing directors and directors of 13 overseas companies, for allegedly embezzling BDT 1,159 crore by sending workers to Malaysia at five times the government-fixed cost; charges are under several Penal Code sections and the Money Laundering Prevention Act.

According to the ACC, the accused formed a syndicate while holding various posts in BAIRA (Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies), ignored the selection and financial conditions of the agreement when sending workers to Malaysia, and laundered the illegal money through transfer and conversion.
facts.source_in_article: ACC Director General Akhtar Hossain / case statement

facts.statement: Earlier, on the same kind of allegation, cases were filed against 12 other companies over about BDT 1,128 crore; in total the ACC has so far taken legal action in 25 cases against 64 accused over about BDT 2,288 crore of alleged embezzlement in Malaysia labour sending.

headline_en: 'Probashi bond': profit on investment, tax-free income and extra security
summary_en: An explainer on the Wage Earner Development Bond ('probashi bond') for Bangladeshis working abroad: interest rates by slab, tax-free profit, death-risk benefit, loans against the bond, the five-year term renewable twice, removal of the investment ceiling from 1 December 2024, who may buy, the documents needed and where to buy.

facts.statement: The Wage Earner Development Bond (known as the 'probashi bond') is a one-time investment with the government by Bangladeshis working abroad, returned with profit after a fixed term, like a bank fixed deposit but with a higher rate, fully tax-free income and death-risk cover.

The Wage Earner Development Bond pays 12 percent simple interest a year, paid every six months (BDT 100,000 invested gives BDT 6,000 after six months, BDT 12,000 a year); it once paid compound interest but now pays simple interest, and the government can raise or lower the rate from time to time.

Wage Earner Development Bond profit slabs: 12 percent on investment up to the equivalent of BDT 15 lakh in foreign currency; 11 percent from BDT 15 lakh 1 to BDT 30 lakh; 10 percent from BDT 30 lakh 1 to BDT 50 lakh; 9 percent from BDT 50 lakh 1 to BDT 1 crore.
No source tax or income tax is payable on Wage Earner Development Bond income, unlike other savings certificates where tax is deducted.

If a Wage Earner Development Bond holder dies before maturity, the nominee gets a death-risk benefit, capped at BDT 20 lakh and only if the holder was under 55; the nominee must apply within three months of the death. The heirs receive the principal and profit at maturity.

A Wage Earner Development Bond can be used as collateral for a bank loan of up to 75 percent of the investment; the loan cannot be taken outside Bangladesh and the bond cannot be used as collateral for a third party.

The Wage Earner Development Bond has a five-year term and, under the government notification, a bond bought with remittance income can be reinvested for two further consecutive terms, so three terms and 15 years in total.

In November 2024 the government removed the investment ceiling on the Wage Earner Development Bond; from 1 December (2024) expatriate Bangladeshis can buy as much as they wish, as was already the case for the US Dollar Premium Bond and US Dollar Investment Bond.

Non-resident Bangladeshi mariners, pilots and cabin crew employed in the overseas offices of foreign-owned shipping and airline companies may invest in the Wage Earner Development Bond; so may government employees working at Bangladesh embassies abroad. The wage earner can invest in their own name or in the name of a person they nominate.

To buy a Wage Earner Development Bond one needs a national ID card, passport, a copy of a valid visa, proof of employment and a savings account in Bangladesh; business people need a trade licence and professionals a professional certificate. A foreign currency (FC) account is not required.
Wage Earner Development Bonds can be bought at Bangladesh Bank, exchange houses, exchange companies, and the foreign and authorised dealer (AD) branches of scheduled banks.

headline_en: 36 Bangladeshis detained: Bangladesh will fully cooperate with Malaysia in the investigation
summary_en: Bangladesh's foreign ministry said on 5 July 2025 it will fully cooperate with Malaysia's investigation of 36 Bangladeshi workers arrested over alleged links to the Islamic State (IS). Five have been charged, 15 are to be sent back, 16 remain in police custody; three have already been returned and are being questioned in Bangladesh.

facts.statement: Malaysia's Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said on 27 June (2025) that 36 Bangladeshis had been arrested for alleged links with the Islamic State (IS) militant group; the Bangladesh foreign ministry says they were arrested in a recent security operation the week before 5 July 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian Home Minister / Bangladesh Ministry of Foreign Affairs

facts.statement: Malaysia's police chief said all the 36 detained Bangladeshis were working in Malaysia's factory, construction and service sectors; they allegedly sent money to IS in Syria and Bangladesh, recruited members by targeting other Bangladeshi workers, and spread extremist ideology through social media and online messaging platforms.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysia's police chief at a Kuala Lumpur press conference, 4 July 2025

facts.statement: Of the 36 Bangladeshis detained in Malaysia over alleged IS links, five have been charged with being members of a terrorist organisation, 15 will be sent back to Bangladesh, and the remaining 16 are still in police custody under investigation.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysia's police chief at a Kuala Lumpur press conference, 4 July 2025

facts.statement: Malaysia's police chief said 100 to 150 people may be involved in the network; those with a low level of involvement will be sent back to their own country and those deeply involved will be dealt with under Malaysian law.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysia's police chief at a Kuala Lumpur press conference, 4 July 2025

facts.statement: After the arrests the Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur contacted the Malaysian authorities and Bangladesh formally asked Malaysia for the identities of those detained and the charges against them; the ministry says the High Commission will give necessary help to expatriate Bangladeshis when needed.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Ministry of Foreign Affairs press release, 5 July 2025

facts.statement: Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul told Prothom Alo on 4 July 2025 that three people had already been sent back from Malaysia and were being interrogated; everyone returned after being detained on this allegation will be interrogated and, if evidence of militancy links is found, put on trial.

headline_en: MoU signed to increase legal migration to Italy
summary_en: On Tuesday 6 May 2025 Bangladesh signed its first 'Migration and Mobility' memorandum of understanding with Italy, signed by adviser Asif Nazrul and Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi in Dhaka. Nazrul also said undocumented women workers in Saudi Arabia have got a chance to be regularised, and that women workers in Jordan who became irregular can regularise without a fine by declaring themselves to the authorities.

facts.statement: On Tuesday 6 May 2025 Bangladesh signed, for the first time, a 'Migration and Mobility' memorandum of understanding with Italy, aimed at stopping irregular migration and increasing legal migration; it was signed at the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment by adviser Professor Asif Nazrul and Italy's Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul said Italy will take workers in two ways, 'seasonal' and 'non-seasonal'; a joint technical committee is planned that will meet once a year, and work is under way on Italian-language training at Technical Training Centres.
Asked how many people can be sent to Italy and in which sectors, Asif Nazrul said the MoU does not contain such details; the current quota will be increased and Italy will consider a quota increase.

At the Italy MoU signing, Bangladesh also discussed making the visa process easier for Bangladeshi students in Italy and removing Bangladesh from the Italian government's high-risk list for migration.
Asif Nazrul said memoranda of understanding have already been signed with six European countries including Portugal and Austria to increase legal migration to Europe.

After a recent visit to Saudi Arabia, Asif Nazrul said an opportunity has been created to regularise women workers living illegally in Saudi Arabia, and that there were fruitful talks with the Saudi government on sending more skilled and unskilled workers from Bangladesh.

Asif Nazrul said women workers in Jordan who became irregular for reasons such as changing their assigned workplace can become legal without a fine by contacting the relevant authority and making an admission; otherwise they will face a large fine.
Asif Nazrul said increasing the number of male workers in Jordan was discussed with the Jordanian government.

headline_en: A remittance fighter's self-reflection in the mirror of 1 May
summary_en: A May Day opinion piece by an expatriate writer arguing that Bangladesh gives returning migrant workers no pension, social insurance or mental-health support, unlike the Philippines' OWWA. He proposes a mandatory remittance pension scheme, reintegration and re-skilling, an entrepreneur fund, health units and national recognition; the rest is general political commentary.

facts.statement: The writer says more than 1.5 crore (15 million) expatriate Bangladeshi workers are spread around the world and send about USD 24 billion a year.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer Rahman Mridha (former director, Pfizer, Sweden)

facts.statement: The writer says most expatriate workers return after working 20 to 30 years and find no permanent social security structure in Bangladesh: no pension, no social insurance, no mental-health support; he contrasts this with the Philippines' Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA).
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer Rahman Mridha (former director, Pfizer, Sweden)

facts.statement: The writer proposes five measures for returning migrants: a mandatory national remittance pension scheme; a reintegration and re-skilling programme with jobs and training; an entrepreneur fund with easy-term loans; specialised mental and physical health units for post-migration crises; and an annual national honour.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer Rahman Mridha (former director, Pfizer, Sweden)

summary_en: On Wednesday 30 April 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission filed a case against former Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Imran Ahmad over BDT 90 lakh of illegal assets and BDT 6 crore of abnormal transactions. He had been arrested on 20 October 2024 and remanded in a human trafficking case filed at Paltan police station.

facts.statement: On Wednesday 30 April 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission (Dudok) filed a case against former Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Imran Ahmad for BDT 90 lakh of illegal assets and BDT 6 crore of abnormal transactions.
facts.source_in_article: ACC Director General (Prevention) Md. Akhtar Hossain

facts.statement: Former expatriates' welfare minister Imran Ahmad was arrested by the Dhaka Metropolitan Detective Branch from Banani, Dhaka on the night of 20 October 2024; the next day he was taken on remand in a case filed at Paltan police station under the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act (a related headline says three days' remand).

Imran Ahmad, five-time MP for Sylhet-4, became State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment in 2018, full minister the next year, and held the same ministry again in the government formed after the 2024 election.

headline_en: Jordan to take 300 women workers through government channel, return airfare also provided
summary_en: State-owned BOESL announced recruitment of 300 women sewing machine operators for Tasker Apparel Company in Jordan, with free accommodation, food and medical care and airfare paid by the employer. The article gives the wage, contract terms, BOESL charges, documents to bring, and the interview on 7 March 2025 at the Women's Technical Training Centre, Mirpur, Dhaka.

facts.statement: Through Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), Tasker Apparel Company (তাস্কার অ্যাপারেল) in Jordan will recruit 300 women workers as female machine operators.

Eligibility for the BOESL Jordan Tasker Apparel machine operator jobs: women aged 20 to 35 with relevant work experience, practical experience of operating plain machines and overlock machines, and proficiency on at least two machines.
Monthly basic pay for the BOESL Jordan Tasker Apparel female machine operator job is stated as BDT 21,311; duty is eight hours a day, six days a week, with overtime available.

The Jordan Tasker Apparel job contract is three years and renewable; the employer pays for accommodation, food, primary medical care and transport, the airfare to join, and the return airfare after three years of satisfactory service; other terms follow Jordan's labour law.

Anyone with a case against them in Bangladesh or Jordan is ineligible for the BOESL Jordan recruitment. Those who previously returned from Jordan need not apply, except those who worked at Tasker company, who can re-apply and attend the interview.

Selected women machine operators for Jordan must pay a BDT 1,000 medical fee, BDT 220 for fingerprints and a BDT 23,500 BOESL service charge, by pay order in the name of "BOESL, Dhaka" from Sonali Bank, Moghbazar branch, submitted at the BOESL office. No additional cost is needed anywhere else.
The BDT 23,500 BOESL service charge will be paid back to the worker by Tasker company three months after she goes to Jordan.
An application fee of BDT 100 is payable for the online application to BOESL for the Jordan jobs.
Interview for the BOESL Jordan Tasker Apparel recruitment: 7 March (2025) at 8 am at the Women's Technical Training Centre (Mohila TTC), Darus Salam Road, Mirpur, Dhaka.

Candidates for the BOESL Jordan interview must bring four passport-size colour photos, the original passport, and four colour sets and four black-and-white sets of photocopies of the passport's photo page; anyone with more than one passport must bring them all. A CV is not needed.
Applying online to BOESL guarantees an interview but not the job; candidates must pass a trade test/examination.
BOESL has no agent or sub-agent and makes worker selection decisions itself.
For information on the BOESL Jordan recruitment: telephone 02-48319125 and 02-48317515, and the Probash Bondhu call centre 16135.

headline_en: Expatriate workers protest in front of T&T Bhaban with six-point demand
summary_en: On Monday 10 February 2025 workers returned from the UAE and other countries rallied in Dhaka with six demands, including rehabilitation, lifting of the UAE 'no entry' on them and a foundation for affected expatriates. They say they were jailed abroad for protesting during Bangladesh's July movement, then released and sent home, and cannot go back.

facts.statement: Returned workers say that when the movement began in Bangladesh in July (2024) they also protested while abroad, were jailed for it, and returned to Bangladesh after release, suffering financial loss.
Workers who returned to Bangladesh from the UAE after being jailed over the July protests say the UAE has put a 'no entry' on them, so they cannot go back to Dubai unless it is lifted.

The protesting returnees say arrests in the UAE in the same case are still continuing and some Bangladeshi expatriates are still held in UAE prisons in that case; they demand diplomatic talks to stop the arrests and bring the prisoners home.

The returnees' six demands: (1) jobs for affected returnees, sending those who wish abroad at government initiative free of cost, interest-free loans for former businesspeople and new entrepreneurs, and government allowances for the elderly; (2) state initiative to lift the UAE no-entry; (3) stop arrests and free those still jailed in the UAE; (4) identify and try those who gave lists of expatriates' names to foreign law enforcement, including diplomats of the time and Consul General B M Jamal; (5) a trust like the July Smriti Foundation to compensate affected expatriates and inclusion of jailed returnees in the list of the July Mass Uprising Directorate under the Liberation War Affairs Ministry; (6) permission for a seven-member delegation to meet the Chief Adviser to invite him to a thanksgiving event.

On Monday 10 February 2025 the returnee workers gathered at about 10:30 am in front of Hotel InterContinental in Dhaka and at about 1:30 pm rallied in front of the T&T Bhaban nearby; a six-member delegation set off to meet the Chief Adviser.

headline_en: Case in Barishal court over alleged trafficking of 23 young men to Saudi Arabia
summary_en: On Monday 28 October 2024 a case was filed at the Barishal Human Trafficking Tribunal against three people, including the managing director of the Dhaka recruiting agency SJ Group, for sending 23 men to Saudi Arabia on a false promise of solar-panel company jobs at 1,800 riyals a month; 12 were caught and deported and 11 are untraced. A separate case filed the day before accuses three people linked to M R International of sending a man to Saudi Arabia, giving him no job and handing him to a gang that demanded BDT 5 lakh ransom.

facts.statement: On Monday 28 October 2024 a case was filed at the Barishal Human Trafficking Offences Tribunal against three people including a recruiting agency director for allegedly trafficking 23 men from Barishal to Saudi Arabia with a promise of high-paid jobs; judge Md. Sohel Ahmed ordered the officer-in-charge of Mehendiganj police station to record it as an FIR and submit an investigation report. The plaintiff is Ershad Howlader of Darichar-Khajuria village, Mehendiganj upazila, father of one of the men.

Accused in the 23-man Saudi trafficking case: Araf Hossain alias Sifat, a Saudi-based expatriate and managing director of recruiting agency SJ Group of Purana Paltan, Dhaka; and Babul Howlader and Kuddus Howlader, sons of Samsul Haque Howlader of Badarpur village, Mehendiganj upazila, Barishal.

The accused lured Hasanuzzaman (son of plaintiff Ershad Howlader) and 22 other young men with jobs at a solar panel firm named in the case as 'Taj Al Nawar Trading East Company' (তাজ আল নাওয়ার ট্রেডিং ইস্ট কোম্পানি) in Saudi Arabia at a monthly salary of 1,800 riyals.

headline_en: A boat journey on the road to death... the chains of this modern slavery are still invisible
summary_en: A feature on sea trafficking from Cox's Bazar/Teknaf towards Malaysia, with accounts from victims and families: a son jailed in Malaysia, a brother missing for seven and a half years, a man jailed nearly a year in Myanmar after his trawler broke down, and another who drifted three months at sea and was held 11 months in Indonesia. It describes broker lures, ransom demands, killings at sea and UNHCR figures on Rohingya sea departures and deaths.

facts.statement: Local brokers mainly target teenagers and young men, promising that it will cost little and that jobs pay a lakh taka a month; better-off people, especially those aged 18 to 35, are also lured with onward travel via Malaysia and Indonesia to Australia, even America or New Zealand; women are told they will get good work in hotels, motels, parlours or shopping malls.

In April (2024) the government brought 173 Bangladeshis home from prison in Myanmar; the article says Mohammad Jamal was among them (though Jamal himself says he returned in July; the article carries both).
Mohammad Jamal of Cox's Bazar agreed a BDT 4 lakh deal with a broker named Ayub to go to Malaysia by sea.

In July 2023 Jamal and nine others were taken in a small boat from Garjania, Ramu upazila, Cox's Bazar and put on a 'ship' that was in fact a small fishing trawler carrying 73 people in all, including five females under 18.

After three days at sea the trawler's hull cracked in Myanmar (Burma) waters; after about two more days the passengers tied a red cloth to the trawler and deliberately surrendered to the Myanmar navy. Rohingya and Bangladeshis were kept in separate prisons; Jamal was held in a jail he calls 'Myo Myo Taung' (মিও মিও টং).

In the Myanmar prison Bangladeshi prisoners were made to do all the work, from growing vegetables to cooking, on scant food: rice starch at about 7 am, some rice with dried chilli at 11 am and rice again at 4 pm, with no fish or meat. Jamal says he served 11 months 19 days and returned with government help in July; those who said they were under 18 were still being held.

Kamal (pseudonym) of Teknaf made a BDT 1 lakh deal with a man named Abu to go to Malaysia, to be repaid after getting a good job there; during the voyage the brokers pressed for BDT 3 lakh ransom, and the total cost by the time he got home was BDT 2 lakh 30 thousand.

Kamal's trawler, carrying Bangladeshis and Rohingya, first reached the Bay of Bengal in Myanmar's waters and stayed seven days, then headed for Malaysia via Thailand; on reaching Malaysia it was chased by Malaysian police into Indonesian waters, and was sent back from there too.

On Kamal's trawler a Rohingya who protested was shot and thrown into the water; two Bengalis died in a clash with Rohingya; people who fell ill and died from lack of food were thrown into the sea; those who asked for food or water were beaten. Food was plain rice with chilli and one glass of water once a day, which had to last 28 hours.

After the Bengalis sank the trawler in anger and many passing ships did not rescue them, an Indonesian navy ship rescued Kamal's group; they were held in Indonesia for 11 months before the Bangladesh government brought them back. He had drifted at sea for three months in all.
Brokers on the sea route torture passengers and collect money from their families as ransom.

Sohel of Karachi Para village, Teknaf boarded a boat to go to Malaysia by sea and went missing; his widowed mother Hasina Akter says the government informed her that he is in prison in Malaysia and will bring him back once all papers are submitted; she has been running between the police station and the magistrate's office.

Manik Molla of Teknaf has been searching for his younger brother Shakil Molla for seven and a half years; Shakil, then 17, left by sea for Malaysia and was never heard from. About two years ago a broker told the family Shakil was in a Malaysian prison; they paid the broker money and he also vanished.
According to UNHCR, 8,312 Rohingya refugees tried to go to Malaysia by sea from 2018 to 2022; 589 of them drowned and many went missing.

Sufia, a 28-year-old Rohingya woman whose marriage was arranged with a Rohingya man in Malaysia, died of dehydration about two days into the boat journey; traffickers had demanded BDT 3 lakh from her relatives to deliver her, and the family learned of her death from someone on the boat while still raising the money.

Anti-trafficking experts stress teaching the public the difference between 'migration' and 'trafficking' and urge people to be open about their plans to go abroad instead of keeping them secret as brokers advise. Victim Kamal tells everyone to try to do something at home rather than go abroad the hard way.
People concerned believe that neither arrests of brokers, deaths in 'gunfights' nor deaths in trawler sinkings have been able to stop human trafficking by sea.

headline_en: How did his father die in Kuwait? Selim has been seeking the answer for 14 years
summary_en: Md. Abdul Ali, a legally employed Bangladeshi driver in Kuwait since 1985, died on 27 November 2010 in Jleeb Al-Shuyoukh; his body came home on 14 January 2011 with head injuries and broken teeth. His son Selim has filed more than 11 applications to Bangladeshi offices over 14 years seeking the cause of death and compensation; the embassy reported that the employer (kafeel) refused to help with compensation, and the Kuwaiti death certificate gives the cause as 'under consideration'.

facts.statement: Bangladeshi worker Md. Abdul Ali died on 27 November 2010 in the Jleeb Al-Shuyoukh (গিলিব আল সুয়েখ) area of Kuwait; his body returned to Bangladesh on 14 January 2011. He had worked in Kuwait as a driver since 1985.

Abdul Ali's brother Abdul Mannan (34 years in Kuwait) and son Selim say the body had injury marks on the head, many broken teeth and blood stains on the beard, and they believe he was tortured and killed rather than dying naturally.
facts.source_in_article: Brother Abdul Mannan and son Selim

facts.statement: Abdul Ali had taken work under a new owner only two months before he died, and was working for an owner other than the employer through whom he had gone to Kuwait; Kuwaiti daily Al Shahid reported on 16 December 2010 on his unnatural death and said he had not been paid for those two months.

Abdul Mannan says that after the death those concerned hurried over the body and suggested burying it in Kuwait; when he considered finding the cause or filing a case he received threats by mobile phone and hints he could be framed in a case, and he got no help from embassy staff of the time.

In a letter dated 7 August 2011 to the BMET director general, the Bangladesh embassy in Kuwait's First Secretary (Labour) K M Ali Reza wrote that the embassy contacted Abdul Ali's kafeel (employer) several times on mobile number 99056231 about compensation/financial benefit, that the kafeel said he could not cooperate on compensation, and that Abdul Ali had been working legally in Kuwait.
facts.source_in_article: Embassy letter by First Secretary (Labour) K M Ali Reza

facts.statement: Selim says the number given in the embassy letter as the kafeel's is actually his uncle Abdul Mannan's number in Kuwait, raising doubt whether the embassy contacted the kafeel at all; his father's phone had two numbers of the kafeel but the embassy did nothing with them.

Selim wrote to the Bangladesh ambassador in Kuwait on 15 January (2024) saying the death certificate from Kuwait's birth and death registration branch does not give the real cause, stating 'condition under consideration' in the cause-of-death field.

Since 2011 Selim has filed more than 11 applications to government offices: on 5 February 2024 to the foreign and expatriates' welfare ministries demanding a fair investigation and maximum compensation, and on 11 February 2024 to the Principal Secretary of the Prime Minister's Office, the Secretary of the expatriates' welfare ministry and the Director General of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board.

The article says BMET asked the Bangladesh embassy in Kuwait on 27 June 2012 to re-investigate, that the embassy's First Secretary (Labour) replied on 7 August of that year, and that Abdul Ali's wife Kawsari Begum, dissatisfied, re-applied to BMET's Director (Welfare) on 4 April 2012 (dates as printed; the article elsewhere dates the embassy letter 7 August 2011).

Mostafa Jamil Khan, Director (Welfare) of the foreign ministry's Consular and Welfare wing, wrote to the Kuwait embassy on 6 February 2024 asking it to take necessary steps; he told Prothom Alo that after so many years it is hard to prove Abdul Ali was murdered in Kuwait.
facts.source_in_article: Mostafa Jamil Khan, Director (Welfare), Ministry of Foreign Affairs

headline_en: Case under migration law for anyone who tries to go abroad illegally
summary_en: Police in Cox's Bazar have begun filing cases under the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act against Rohingya who flee the camps to go to Malaysia or elsewhere by sea. In the first such case, three Rohingya girls aged 12 and 14 rescued from a boat at Teknaf on 5 January 2024 were sent to jail along with an alleged trafficker, then bailed on 9 January and ordered back to the camp.

facts.statement: Police in Cox's Bazar say Rohingya who flee the Ukhiya camps and try to go to Malaysia or another country by sea will now be charged under the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act and sent to jail; police say the step is meant to stop human trafficking and risky illegal sea crossings.

On the night of 6 January 2024 Sub-Inspector Sanjib Kumar Pal filed a case at Teknaf Model police station under the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act against three Rohingya girls (two aged 12, one aged 14, from Balukhali camp, Ukhiya) and two alleged traffickers; all those held were sent to the district jail through the court. It is reported to be the first such case against a Rohingya who fled a camp.

The arrested alleged trafficker is Ariful Islam (19), son of Abdu Sattar of Adharghona village, Kalamarchhara union, Maheshkhali; Shamshul Alam (38), son of Amir Hamza of Lengurbil village, Teknaf Sadar union, is also accused and is absconding.

On the afternoon of 5 January 2024 at Lambarighat on the Teknaf Marine Drive, assistant judge Maitri Bhattacharya, returning from election inquiry duty, saw three Rohingya girls being put on a wooden boat for illegal trafficking to Malaysia; police with her rescued them, Teknaf police detained the trafficker and seized the boat.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Saiful Islam, bench clerk of the Cox's Bazar assistant judge court

facts.statement: Teknaf OC Muhammad Osman Gani said the three girls admitted in initial questioning that they were going abroad of their own will, which is why they were also charged. The Cox's Bazar children's court granted them bail on Tuesday 9 January 2024; they were to be sent back to the camp on 10 January and must appear in court from the camp as accused.
facts.source_in_article: Teknaf OC Muhammad Osman Gani; jail superintendent Md. Shah Alam Khan

facts.statement: According to police and Rohingya leaders, in the last five years law enforcers rescued at least 5,000 Rohingya being trafficked by trawler to Malaysia from the coasts of Teknaf, Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar Sadar and Maheshkhali and returned them to the camps, and returned at least 60,000 Rohingya caught fleeing to other districts; no case was filed against any of them before.
There are 12.5 lakh registered Rohingya in 33 camps in Ukhiya and Teknaf, of whom 8 lakh came in the months after 25 August 2017.

headline_en: No contact with family for four months, then a friend's message from Russia: 'Sagar is no more'
summary_en: Mohammad Sagar, 24, of Chandina, Cumilla went to Russia in mid-2025 for BDT 6 lakh and worked in a bakery, then was lured by a Bangladeshi broker in Russia into the Russian army and was sent to the Ukraine war in May 2026. His family lost contact, and on Saturday 17 October 2026 a friend in Russia messaged that 'Sagar is no more'; the death is unconfirmed.

facts.statement: Mohammad Sagar of Chhaykot, Chandina municipality, Cumilla went to Russia in mid-2025 at a cost of BDT 6 lakh with the help of Sohel, a shop manager and returnee migrant he knew; his father borrowed heavily to send him.
In Russia Sagar worked in a bakery and was earning about BDT 70,000 a month.

A Bangladeshi man Sagar met in Russia promised him a job in the Russian army and a one-time payment of BDT 30 lakh; lured by this, Sagar left the bakery job in May 2026 and joined the Russia-Ukraine war. His uncle says the broker gave false information to enlist him as a soldier although Sagar is illiterate.

After Sagar was sent to the Ukraine war in May 2026 his family lost contact; on Saturday 17 October 2026 his friend Rajon, who is in Russia, sent a message to Sagar's sister's phone saying only 'Sagar is no more', gave no details and could not be reached afterwards. The family cannot confirm the death, or when and how it happened.
Before going to the war Sagar sent BDT 3 lakh to his uncle Abdul Awal's bank account; contact stopped after that.

Chandina Upazila Nirbahi Officer Mohammad Ashraful Haque said on 19 October 2026 that he sent municipality staff to the family's house, that there is no confirmed information of Sagar's death other than the friend's message, and that they are keeping track.

headline_en: Remittances below USD 300 crore for four months running; USD 276 crore came in September
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank's update shows remittances of USD 276.60 crore in September 2026, down from USD 296.66 crore in August but 3 percent above September 2025. Fiscal 2025-26 set a record at USD 3,559 crore.

facts.statement: Bangladesh received USD 276 crore 60 lakh in remittances in September 2026, down from USD 296 crore 66 lakh in August 2026 but 3 percent more than the USD 268 crore 60 lakh received in September 2025.
Monthly remittances to Bangladesh have been below USD 300 crore for four months in a row; the last month above USD 300 crore was May (2026). July 2026 brought USD 285 crore 87 lakh.
Expatriates sent a record USD 3,559 crore in remittances in fiscal year 2025-26; in 6 of its 12 months remittances exceeded USD 300 crore.
After the political changeover remittances through banks grew by about 27 percent in fiscal year 2024-25, exceeding USD 30 billion for the first time.
Sector people say the ease of sending money through the banking channel and the stable official dollar rate are keeping remittance inflow positive.
